contributions.headingText: Mycosis fungoides is a primary cutaneous T-cell lymphoma clinically characterized by the sequential evolution of patches, plaques, and tumours, and pathologically comprising infiltrates of clonal small to medium-sized mature T cells with hyperconvoluted nuclei, which are epitheliotropic in most cases.

Folliculotropic mycosis fungoides; pagetoid reticulosis; granulomatous slack skin disease

Skin lesions of mycosis fungoides can be one or a few localized lesions, or they can be multiple, widespread, and sometimes even confluent. When localized, they often occur in sun-protected areas, like skin flexures (axillae, groins) and the lower trunk / buttocks (bathing-trunk distribution). Extracutaneous dissemination occurs exclusively in the latest stages of the disease, initially involving draining lymph nodes, and occasionally with more extensive spread to viscera and blood {5009530}.

Mycosis fungoides is characterized by an indolent clinical course over years or decades, with persisting, slowly growing lesions. Early-stage mycosis fungoides manifests with patches and plaques {16310068}, whereas advanced stage mycosis fungoides characteristically shows progression to nodules/tumours or erythroderma.

Mycosis fungoides patches are erythematous and scaling. The skin may look finely wrinkled and thinner than normal. Mycosis fungoides plaques are variably infiltrated and scaling, with a red to brown hue. Patches and plaques are sharply demarcated, annular to arciform, and polycyclic; they might occur separately or simultaneously in the same patient. In dark skin, lesions show dyschromia and are often hypopigmented rather than erythematous, although occasionally they are hyperpigmented or poikilodermatous {31499157}. Tumours generally arise in advanced disease, typically occurring in patients with a long history of patches and plaques. Tumours may become eroded and may ulcerate.

Bacterial superinfection is common in the advanced stages of the disease; it is much rarer in the early stages. Skin, soft tissue infections, and pneumonia are frequent causes of sepsis in these patients and a major cause of hospitalization and death {30098016}.

Subtypes of mycosis fungoides deviate from the classic clinical course. The clinical and histological features of these subtypes are described in Histopathology, below.

Mycosis fungoides is the most common type of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, accounting for > 50% of cases, with an incidence of 5.8 cases per 1 million person-years {24438969; 32141115}. Mycosis fungoides can occur at any age; the peak incidence is in the late fifties {31465745}, but it can also arise in children and adolescents (4–11% of mycosis fungoides cases) {31630432; 33656521}. The M:F ratio is 2:1 {24438969}. In the current literature, most reported cases (77.7%) are in White people; however, the number of cases of mycosis fungoides in Black people is disproportionately high relative to population {28645647}. Among Black people, mycosis fungoides seems to have a female predilection, a worse prognosis, and an earlier onset {28645647; 31623818; 25458019}.

No clear etiological factor has been identified {32477957}. Data showing that transient antibiotic treatment is associated with a decrease in fraction of neoplastic T cells, cell proliferation, and STAT3 signalling suggest that the microbiome may be involved in the evolution of a malignant clone {31331920}. Early mycosis fungoides is thought to be mediated by contact with immature antigen-presenting cells leading to constitutive T-cell receptor (TCR) activation, which along with defects in the apoptosis pathway may lead to early clonal expansion of T cells, contributing to the evolution of disease {27717961; 11929784}.

Recent next-generation sequencing data have identified genetic aberrations in signalling pathways and epigenetic processes that may contribute to the pathogenesis of mycosis fungoides, i.e. in the context of chronic antigenic stimulation of skin-resident T lymphocytes {27717961; 11929784}. Alteration of tumour suppressor pathways {26258847; 26192916; 26551667}, and/or constitutive T-cell activation, chromatin modification, cell-cycle regulation, and alterations of NF-κB signalling downstream to TCR may be involved in regulating T-cell survival and proliferation {29981755; 28694326}. Alterations of the JAK-3/STAT3 and MAPK signal transduction pathways may contribute to the survival and proliferation of malignant T cells in mycosis fungoides {27540476; 20213502; 15141228; 31049933; 28182501; 21209378}. Hypomethylation and hypermethylation signatures have been observed in mycosis fungoides; for example DNMT3A, a gene encoding a methyltransferase, is often mutated or deleted in mycosis fungoides, signifying that genetic aberrations may underlie epigenetic dysregulation {32477957; 29981755}. No specific chromosomal translocations have to date been identified in mycosis fungoides.

The histological features differ with disease stage. Early-stage (“patch”) lesions are characterized by subtle epidermotropic infiltrates of small to medium-sized haloed lymphocytes with hyperchromatic, hyperconvoluted (cerebriform) nuclei, lining up along the basal and low-mid layers of the epidermis, often associated with a mild to dense band of reactive small lymphocytes and admixed histiocytes. As the lesions transition to “plaque”-stage disease, lymphocytes may more prominently colonize both upper layers of the epidermis, in a pagetoid pattern or forming clusters or “collections” (Pautrier microabscesses) tightly associated with Langerhans cell scaffolding. Granulomatous infiltrates can be present, and they may even obscure the diagnostic lymphoid infiltrates, delaying care {19075143; 23685027}. Mycosis fungoides tumours often fail to display the hallmark feature of epidermotropism, instead filling the dermis as diffuse sheets of small, medium-sized, and large atypical cells.

Large cell transformation, defined by the presence of > 25% large lymphoid cells, or aggregates of large cells in dermal infiltrates, may herald (and is commonly associated with) disease progression. The designation of large cell transformation has poor interobserver reproducibility {29543675}, possibly due to the dense tumoural lesions in which it most commonly occurs.

Biopsies of enlarged lymph nodes are often performed for staging purposes. Enlarged lymph nodes from patients with mycosis fungoides frequently show dermatopathic lymphadenopathy with paracortical expansion due to the large number of histiocytes, some containing melanin pigment, as well as Langerhans and interdigitating cells with abundant, pale cytoplasm. Early involvement by mycosis fungoides cells may be difficult to identify in nodal tissue and may require flow cytometric evaluation and molecular studies for TR gene clonality; however, in higher N stage disease, the normal architecture of the nodes becomes effaced by malignant cells that are clearly recognizable {17540844}.

Immunophenotype

Classic mycosis fungoides demonstrates a CD2+, CD3+, TCRβ+, CD5+, CD4+, CD8− phenotype. CD7 is often dimly expressed or partially lost, particularly in advanced disease. CD30 may be positive or negative, and as with other pan–T-cell antigens, may show varied levels of expression in contemporaneous and subsequent biopsies {35403270}. Cutaneous lymphocyte antigen (CLA) and CCR4 {14708605}, both associated with lymphocyte homing to the skin, are expressed in most cases. Antigens suggestive of immune exhaustion (PD1), also common to T follicular helper (TFH) cells, are frequent in mycosis fungoides; however, other markers of TFH phenotype are rare. TOX may be an adjunct marker distinguishing early-stage mycosis fungoides {22377759}. Advanced-stage mycosis fungoides may show numerous immunophenotypic aberrancies, including loss of the pan–T-cell antigens CD2 and CD5, diminution of CD4, or loss of TCRβ expression, as well as partial expression of CD30 (which may be absent to diffuse). Aggregates of B cells may be identified within these tumoural infiltrates, and Ki-67 labels greater percentages of neoplastic cells.

Clinically classic mycosis fungoides with a cytotoxic phenotype (CD8+ and/or TCRγδ) is well recognized. Of note, CD8-positive paediatric mycosis fungoides and CD8-positive hypopigmented mycosis fungoides, common in Black and Asian populations, may be associated with a more indolent course {26262921; 23379648; 28676328; 31499157; 33911704}.

Nuclear expression of phosphorylated STAT3 can be found in a high proportion of mycosis fungoides / Sézary syndrome cases regardless of JAK mutation {21818116}.

Folliculotropic mycosis fungoides

This subtype comprises cases of folliculotropic mycosis fungoides with or without adnexal involvement beyond the hair follicles, which may occasionally present as predominantly syringotropic mycosis fungoides. The presentation is most common on the head and neck, upper extremities, and thorax. Alopecia, pruritus, and palmar/plantar lesions are characteristic {18559762}. Folliculotropic mycosis fungoides may have a worse disease course than classic mycosis fungoides, unless it is of an early-stage pattern versus more advance tumour-like disease {33295938; 29726638; 27245278; 27276223; 28132406}. Infiltrated plaques, acneiform lesions (comedo-like), and follicular keratosis pilaris–like lesions have been noted to be prominent features in folliculotropic mycosis fungoides {20079954}.

In folliculotropic mycosis fungoides, atypical lymphocytes infiltrate the follicular epithelium, typically sparing the interfollicular epidermis. Eosinophils are frequently seen in the perifollicular area. As identified on clinical examination, cystic dilation or cornified plugging may be confirmed microscopically. Follicular mucinosis and hyperplastic eccrine structures are common, with mucinous degeneration of the follicular epithelium occurring in 60% of cases {30098016}, ranging from widened intercellular spaces to large mucin lakes. Staging of the infiltrates enables prognostic and therapeutic stratification. Specifically, folliculotropic mycosis fungoides should be distinguished as either mild (early stage) or exuberant (advanced stage). Advanced-stage infiltrates comprise dense dermal interfollicular involvement {33295938; 29726638; 27245278; 27276223; 28132406}. An intermediate plaque-stage group of folliculotropic mycosis fungoides can be stratified into better or worse outcome groups by large cell size, higher Ki-67 index, interfollicular epidermotropism, and absent follicular mucinosis {31755567}. Immunophenotypically, folliculotropic mycosis fungoides is CD4-positive.

Pagetoid reticulosis

Pagetoid reticulosis (formerly referred to as Woringer–Kolopp disease) is a slowly growing, well-circumscribed, solitary psoriasiform or keratotic plaque (or localized plaques) affecting the distal extremities or trunk and occurring at any age. Only exceptional cases show disease progression {24666254}, but such cases do not eventuate in death or extracutaneous disease. Histologically, pagetoid reticulosis shows sponge-like disaggregation of the epidermis by small to medium-sized lymphocytes, with additional epidermal changes (hyperplasia, acanthosis, hyperkeratosis). These intraepidermally located lymphocytes display atypical medium-sized to large cerebriform nuclei. They characteristically contrast with an underlying infiltrate of small lymphocytes at the dermoepidermal junction, which lack cytological atypia.

The florid scatter of CD8-positive atypical lymphocytes in all levels of the epidermis (pagetosis) {24666254} is typical. CD4/CD8-negative or CD4-positive cases are rarely identified {10824921}. CD30 may be expressed.

Clinical correlation is necessary to distinguish indolent pagetoid reticulosis from a CD8-positive aggressive epidermotropic cytotoxic T-cell lymphoma.

Granulomatous slack skin disease

Granulomatous slack skin disease is exceedingly rare and arises predominantly in young adult patients with pendulous skin in the axillae, groin, and gluteal folds, with pruritus, erythema, and patches and plaques in skin segments {34649654; 19075143; 22435618}, sometimes in the context of another lymphoma. Atypically, a few cases involve blood, lymph nodes, or viscera. Treatment is challenging, and although the disease is mostly indolent, patients occasionally succumb to it {33656521; 34649654; 19075143}. Granulomatous slack skin disease is characterized by a CD3+, CD4+, CD45RO+ atypical lymphocytic infiltrate; however, the hallmark features are of a granulomatous infiltrate with loss of elastic fibres and numerous multinucleated CD14+, CD68+ monocytes with many nuclei arranged in a wreath-like pattern. Elastophagocytosis can be seen, and elastic stain can highlight the destruction of elastic fibres throughout the dermis {11411914; 22435618}.

FNAB does not play a role in the initial diagnosis of mycosis fungoides. Later in the course of the disease, FNAB may be used to sample skin nodules or parenchymal lesions to obtain material for ancillary testing, to look for morphological evidence of large cell transformation {18798522; 24393425; 22555537}, or to guide site selection for excisional lymph node biopsy {10874888; 17540844}.

Like for other T-cell lymphomas, demonstration of a clonal TR gene rearrangement can be crucial in the diagnosis of mycosis fungoides {26446955; 22918122; 29636372; 34424321; 26048061}. However, clonality results should be carefully interpreted in the proper clinicopathological context, because monoclonal TR clones can be detected in some elderly individuals or in those with autoimmune diseases or chronic dermatoses {17638739; 11229519; 8294871}. In contrast, early mycosis fungoides may yield false negative results {26446955; 18201238}. Matching clones identified at different sites (e.g. blood and skin or two skin sites) are diagnostically helpful {29477101}.

Essential in early-stage mycosis fungoides: presence of persistent and/or progressive patches and plaques, especially in sun-protected areas; presence of small to medium-sized atypical T cells with hyperchromatic, hyperconvoluted (cerebriform) nuclei, preferentially in the epidermis.

Essential in tumour-stage mycosis fungoides: evidence of concurrent or preceding patches and plaques with histological features characteristic of mycosis fungoides.

Desirable: loss of pan–T-cell antigens; demonstration of clonal TR gene rearrangements in skin biopsy in selected cases.

Staging of mycosis fungoides and Sézary syndrome is performed according to the International Society for Cutaneous Lymphomas (ISCL) / European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer (EORTC) system, which stratifies cases into 10 overall clinical stages with consideration of the tumour, node, metastasis, and blood (TNMB) stage [[WHO Classification of Tumours Editorial Board. Haematolymphoid tumours. Lyon (France): International Agency for Research on Cancer; 2024. (WHO classification of tumours series, 5th ed.; vol. 11). https://publications.iarc.who.int/637.]] {17540844}. For classification of the blood and lymph node stages, T-cell clonality testing is necessary {17540844}. Nodal status should be estimated only from clinically abnormal peripheral lymph nodes, defined as nodules ≥ 15 mm or as firm, clustered, or fixed palpable nodes regardless of size {17540844; 15459015; 3876976; 7350998}. Histopathological staging for clinically abnormal lymph nodes is specified in the Haematolymphoid tumours volume [[WHO Classification of Tumours Editorial Board. Haematolymphoid tumours. Lyon (France): International Agency for Research on Cancer; 2024. (WHO classification of tumours series, 5th ed.; vol. 11). https://publications.iarc.who.int/637.]] {17540844; 15459015; 3876976; 7350998}.

Clinical stage, as assessed by TNMB classification, is the key prognostic factor for both disease progression and survival, with tumour stage, as well as blood, lymph node, and visceral involvement, correlating with a poor prognosis. Patients with limited disease generally have an excellent prognosis, with survival similar to that in the general population. Imaging is usually not recommended in early-stage mycosis fungoides {17540844}. In the advanced stages of disease, CT or PET-CT, with or without contrast medium, may be indicated at the time of disease progression (before initiation of chemotherapy) and to evaluate visceral response or progression after a full treatment course. Ultrasound may be of help in the interpretation of lymph node enlargement. Factors correlating with worse survival include the presence of a circulating clone in the absence of phenotypic evidence of blood involvement, older age at diagnosis (> 60 years), elevated lactose dehydrogenase, and folliculotropism {20855822; 25458019; 23735705; 26438120}.
